talkTrack: SOCi is publicly claiming more than 412,000 deployed AI “agents” handling 27 million marketing tasks a year, and prospects evaluating reputation or local-marketing tools will bring those numbers into the room. But two live deals this month tell a different story: buyers picked SOCi mainly on price, then found it missing benchmarks, scoring, leaderboards, and accountability tracking, and are now looking elsewhere or dropping it from scope. The number that matters isn't how many agents SOCi deployed — it's whether an operator can see, benchmark, and act on what those agents produce. Ask the operations leader: when SOCi flags something worth fixing at a property, who actually sees that result, and what happens next?
coverageGaps: This edition draws on the September 22 weekly digest, this week's Monday digest (Sept 28), and field reports posted September 18–27. It is a targeted refresh after a gap in weekly updates to the app itself (the last full item set was dated August 11) rather than a from-scratch sweep of all 104 competitors — the next scheduled sweep continues building on this.
doNotMisdate: The RealPage Federal Register filing below is the DOJ's proposed final judgment, published September 18, 2026 — not the same as the May 8, 2026 response-to-public-comments filing, and not the earlier $218M batch of operator settlements (EQR, Camden, MAA) from May 2026, which is a separate, already-closed matter.
SOCi's 400,000+ agent count is current as of its September 22, 2026 announcement. Treat any higher number a prospect cites as SOCi's own later marketing, not something we've independently verified.

items.headline: SOCi passes 400,000 deployed AI agents, but buyers who chose it on price are finding it can't benchmark or hold anyone accountable
items.summary: SOCi announced it has surpassed 400,000 deployed “Genius Agents” handling local marketing tasks such as review responses and social posting, and cited a G2 ranking of No. 7 among AI agent products for business operations. Internally, two live deals this quarter went to SOCi on price, then the buyer came back looking for benchmarks, scoring, leaderboards, and accountability tracking that the platform doesn't provide.
items.soWhat: SOCi's agent count is a real number and prospects will bring it into the room, but it answers “how much did SOCi do,” not “was it any good, compared to what.” Ask the operations leader who actually sees what an agent flags at a property, and what happens next — that's the gap between marketing automation and a performance layer.

items.headline: DOJ's proposed final judgment against RealPage published in the Federal Register; states say it doesn't end their own claims
items.summary: The Department of Justice's proposed final judgment and competitive impact statement in United States v. RealPage was published in the Federal Register on September 18, opening a public comment period and formalizing terms that restrict certain revenue-management software use by named co-defendant property managers and require a designated antitrust compliance officer. Separately, state attorneys general have told the court their own state-law claims survive the federal settlement and aren't resolved by it.
items.soWhat: This isn't over when the federal settlement closes — state claims are running on their own clock. Any operator still running RealPage's pricing tools should be asked plainly what their compliance sign-off looks like today, and whether they're tracking state-level exposure separately from the federal case.

items.headline: Entrata relaunched its LMS at its user conference: free base content, an upcharge for compliance and custom content
items.summary: A field report from Entrata's conference: the relaunched LMS's base content is included, but fair housing and other compliance content, or custom content, carries an additional charge. Entrata reportedly said onstage they'd “partnered with a best in class provider for compliance content” — that partner is not Grace Hill and wasn't named; the working assumption is it's still Docebo underneath. The attendee also felt the release is still missing functionality.
items.soWhat: If a prospect says Entrata “now has an LMS with compliance content built in,” the accurate follow-up is: whose compliance content, at what extra cost, and kept current how. Treat this as unconfirmed packaging, not a finished platform, until we see it directly.

items.headline: Rilla's disclosed price: $2,650 per agent/year, five-agent minimum, paid in full upfront
items.summary: A client shared Rilla's pricing directly: a five-leasing-agent minimum at $2,650 per agent per year, with the full contract due upfront. The client found the terms unreasonable and too expensive, and passed.
items.soWhat: This is a real, named price point rather than an estimate — useful the next time a prospect is comparing Rilla to a coaching or mystery-shopping program on cost alone. The upfront, full-contract payment term is itself worth surfacing before a prospect gets a quote.

items.headline: Rilla is advertising heavily and expanding into new-construction homebuilder sales training
items.summary: Team members are seeing a marked increase in Rilla's advertising, plus reports it's being adopted by new-construction homebuilders for sales training — a market adjacent to, but distinct from, multifamily leasing.
items.soWhat: Rising visibility means more prospects will bring Rilla up unprompted, even outside multifamily leasing. Worth confirming whether the homebuilder use case changes their multifamily roadmap or pricing, or is a separate product motion entirely.
